opus-5.5.text:
I think a lot of people talk about the data flywheel as if it's automatic: you have users, users generate data, data makes the model better, the better model attracts more users. In practice, I think very few companies actually have a working flywheel, and it's worth asking why.

To me there are a few conditions you need.

First, you need a **reward signal**, not just data. Most applications collect a lot of interaction logs, but logs alone don't tell you what was good or bad. If a user chats with your product for ten minutes, was that because it was helpful or because it was confusing? You need some signal that's actually aligned with the user's real goal. In some domains that's natural. In coding, did the code run, did the user accept the change? In customer service, was the issue resolved? In many consumer chat settings it's very noisy, and then the flywheel is weak.

Second, you need the **ability to actually train on it**. This sounds obvious, but if you're only calling an API from a foundation model company, the data you collect doesn't easily flow back into the model. You can use it for prompt engineering, retrieval, product iteration, which is valuable, but it isn't the same as a model-level flywheel. So either you have your own training capability, or you're in a setup where that signal can really improve the system end to end.

Third, and I think this is the most underrated part, the **task has to be differentiated** from what the general model is already learning. If your users are doing things that look like everyone else's usage, the foundation model companies have far more of that data than you. Your flywheel only matters if you own a distribution of tasks, context, or feedback that others don't have: a specific workflow, a specific environment, a specific kind of user intent.

So in a way, I'd frame it less as "data flywheel" and more as "do you own an environment and an evaluation that others don't?" In what I call the second half of AI, the bottleneck is less about the method and more about defining the right tasks and the right evaluation. A company that has real users doing real tasks, with a clear signal about success, is essentially sitting on a valuable environment. If it can close the loop from that signal back into the model, that's a real moat.

But I'd also be honest: for many applications today, the bigger lever is still the base model getting better. If your product improves mostly because the underlying model got upgraded, then your flywheel isn't really the main driver. The interesting question for a startup is how to design the product so that its own users generate the signal that makes it uniquely better over time. That's a product design problem as much as a research problem.

r001.rationale: The response says that for many applications the larger improvement comes from the underlying model, distinguishing that from a flywheel driven by the product’s own user signals.

r002.rationale: It identifies having one’s own training capability, or another setup that lets the signal improve the system, as a prerequisite.

r003.rationale: It says interaction logs alone do not show what was good or bad and calls for a reward signal that identifies success, with examples such as code running or an issue being resolved.

r004.rationale: The response requires a signal aligned with the user’s real goal, but does not clearly connect the optimized reward to the application’s business success.

r005.rationale: It says the flywheel must involve differentiated tasks, contexts, or feedback that general models do not already learn at scale.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the phrase "data flywheel" gets used a lot, but very few application companies actually have one. So let me try to be concrete about what I think the real ingredients are.

The first thing is that you need a task where the outcome is actually observable. This sounds obvious, but it's the thing most people skip. If a user asks your product to do something, and you can't tell whether it worked, then you're not collecting data, you're collecting logs. A flywheel needs a signal. In coding, that signal is pretty natural: did the code run, did the tests pass, did the user accept the diff or throw it away. In customer support, it's whether the ticket got resolved or escalated. In a lot of consumer chat products, honestly, the signal is very weak. People say "thanks" or they close the tab, and you don't really know what happened. So the first question I'd ask any application company is: what is the feedback, and how fast does it come back? If the loop takes three months, it's not a flywheel.

The second thing is that the data has to actually change the model's behavior, not just sit in a dashboard. This is where I think there's a split. A lot of companies collect feedback and use it for prompt engineering, or for picking which base model to call. That's fine, but it's not compounding. The compounding happens when you can turn the outcome signal into training signal, whether that's fine-tuning, RL, or even just building really good evals that let you iterate much faster than anyone else. If your "flywheel" is just that you have more users so you have more anecdotes, a competitor with a better base model catches up immediately.

The third ingredient, and this is the one I think is most underrated, is that the distribution of tasks has to be yours. If you're a thin wrapper and your users are asking general questions, the lab that makes the base model sees the same distribution, and they have far more data than you do. You don't have an advantage; you have a disadvantage. The flywheel only works when the tasks are specific enough that the frontier labs don't have them, and valuable enough that users keep coming back to generate more. Cursor is a good example here. The data about how real engineers actually edit code in a real repository, what they accept, what they revert, that's a distribution you can't get from the open internet.

And then there's a fourth thing which is more about the organization than the data. You need people who can actually close the loop, meaning people who understand both the product and the training side. Many application companies have great product people and they hire an ML team that sits off to the side, and the two never really talk. Then the data gets collected but nobody knows how to use it, or the ML team trains something that doesn't match what users want. The companies that are winning right now tend to have the loop very tight, sometimes the same person on both sides.

I'd also add a bit of a caveat. I think people assume the flywheel is about model quality, and sometimes it isn't. Sometimes what you accumulate is not training data but context: the user's codebase, their documents, their history, their preferences. That's a kind of data moat too, and in the agent era it might matter more than fine-tuning, because the agent's quality depends enormously on what it knows about this specific user's environment. So I'd broaden the question a bit. It's not just "how do I get data to train a better model." It's "how do I get into a position where my product knows something no one else knows, and gets better at using it every time someone uses it."

r001.rationale: It contrasts companies that collect feedback for prompt or model selection with a compounding flywheel, and notes that a better base model can quickly catch a thin wrapper.

r002.rationale: It describes turning outcomes into training signals, but does not make a company’s ability to train models itself a prerequisite; it also presents evals and accumulated user context as other ways to improve.

r003.rationale: It says outcomes must be observable and gives interaction-derived signals such as tests passing, users accepting code, or support tickets being resolved.

r004.rationale: It identifies useful outcome signals and valuable tasks, but does not clearly require the optimized reward to align with the application’s business success.

r005.rationale: It says general questions expose a company to the same task distribution as the base-model lab, which has more data, and recommends specific tasks that frontier labs do not have.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is to work backward from improvement: what data would actually make your product better, and does using your product naturally generate that data? Having more users and more logs doesn’t automatically give you a data flywheel.

You need a useful feedback signal. If a user asks a question and the model gives an answer, you have a conversation, but you may not know whether the answer was good. In a coding application, you might see whether the code passes tests, whether the user accepts the change, or how they edit it. Those signals give you a better starting point, although none is perfect by itself.

Then you need a way to turn that feedback into improvements. That could mean training a model, but it could also mean improving retrieval, tools, or the workflow. And you need evaluations that tell you whether those changes actually help users.

So I’d look for a fairly specific task where you can observe outcomes and improve repeatedly. The flywheel is only real when usage produces useful feedback, that feedback improves the product, and the improvement gives people a reason to use it more.

r001.rationale: The response says more users and logs do not automatically create a flywheel, but does not distinguish companies’ reliance on underlying-model improvements from having their own flywheel.

r002.rationale: It presents model training as one possible improvement method and explicitly allows alternatives; it does not make a company’s ability to train models a prerequisite.

r003.rationale: It calls for useful feedback from product interactions and gives outcome signals—such as tests passing, user acceptance, and edits—that help indicate whether an output was good.

r004.rationale: It connects feedback to product improvement and repeat usage, but does not identify alignment between the optimized reward and the application’s business success.

r005.rationale: It does not discuss focusing on a relatively non-core capability or explain that general model training might otherwise improve that capability.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is to close the loop between usage, feedback, and improvement. Having lots of users doesn’t automatically give you a data flywheel. You need users to generate information that tells you what the system should do better, and you need a way to turn that information into a better product.

For example, if a user asks a question and gets an answer, that interaction alone may not tell you whether the answer was useful. But if they edit the answer, choose between alternatives, or complete a task successfully, you have a much stronger signal. So the product design matters: can you observe the outcome, not just the request?

Then you need an improvement process. That could mean training a model, but it could also mean improving retrieval, tools, or how the application handles a particular workflow. The important thing is that more usage produces better signals, those signals improve performance, and that improvement gives people a reason to use the product more.

I’d probably start with a narrow task where success is measurable. It’s much easier to build that loop when you know what a good result looks like.

r001.rationale: The response describes a usage-to-improvement loop but does not distinguish companies’ reliance on underlying model improvements from having their own data flywheel.

r002.rationale: It says training a model is one possible improvement method and also names alternatives; it does not make training models oneself a prerequisite.

r003.rationale: It identifies interaction-derived signals—such as edits, choices, and successful task completion—as stronger evidence of usefulness than a request alone, and places those signals in the improvement loop.

r004.rationale: The response does not connect the reward or signal being optimized to the application’s business success.

r005.rationale: The response does not say the flywheel should focus on a relatively non-core capability or contrast it with capability gains from general model training.
